cards.head: Pathologists often disagree when grading dysplasia
cards.take: This meta-analysis pooled eight studies in which 46 pathologists graded the same oral dysplasia slides. Agreement between pathologists was poor: kappa 0.14 with the three-grade WHO system and 0.31 with the simpler high/low-risk binary system. Even the same pathologist regraded slides inconsistently. Chairside: treat a dysplasia grade as an estimate, and seek a second opinion when it would change management.
cards.rib: Ask for a second opinion when the grade will change your plan

cards.head: Brush cytology is accurate, but still not a biopsy
cards.take: This review pooled 53 studies with 13,249 patients comparing oral brush cytology against biopsy histology. Cytology caught about 91% of cancers and potentially malignant lesions and correctly cleared 96% of benign ones; liquid-based samples did slightly better. Studies varied widely. Chairside: cytology can help triage or monitor a lesion when biopsy is refused, but a scalpel biopsy still confirms the diagnosis.
cards.rib: Use cytology to triage or monitor; confirm with tissue biopsy

cards.head: Full excision upgraded nearly half of biopsy diagnoses
cards.take: In 31 Australian patients whose potentially malignant lesions were first sampled by incisional biopsy, each lesion was later fully removed by CO2 laser. The final diagnosis was worse in 14 (45%): 9 (29%) had an unexpected cancer and 5 more had worse dysplasia. A small sample can miss the worst area. Chairside: a mild report on a large lesion does not close the case.
cards.rib: Do not let a mild report on a big lesion stop the referral

cards.head: Black hairy tongue is harmless and usually reversible
cards.take: Black hairy tongue is overgrowth of the filiform papillae, which can reach 12-18 mm instead of under 1 mm. Prevalence ranges from 0.6% to 11.3% in surveys, and men are affected about three times as often. Smoking, tea or coffee, poor hygiene, dry mouth and antibiotics are common triggers. Chairside: reassure, remove the trigger and advise gentle tongue scraping; it is not a precancer.
cards.rib: Reassure, remove the trigger and teach gentle tongue cleaning

cards.ev: Cohort study · Int J Environ Res Public Health 2016
cards.head: Smoker's gum pigmentation fades after quitting
cards.take: This Japanese study scored gum pigmentation on photos of 263 patients from 16 dental clinics. Over several years, pigmented sites fell from 25.6% to 12.8% in those who quit smoking, against a smaller drop from 26.7% to 19.9% in those who kept smoking. Smoker's melanosis is benign. Chairside: show smokers their brown gums as a visible, reversible sign and use it to motivate quitting.
cards.rib: Point out smoker's melanosis and use it to motivate quitting

cards.ev: Retrospective study · J Pre Clin Clin Res 2020
cards.head: Frictional keratosis showed no dysplasia or cancer
cards.take: This Polish review of 176 white-lesion biopsies found no dysplasia or cancer in any of the 63 lesions clinically called frictional keratosis. By contrast, 4 of the 36 lesions called leukoplakia were already cancers. Frictional white patches sit at a rubbing source such as a sharp cusp or cheek biting. Chairside: remove the cause, review shortly after, and biopsy if it persists.
cards.rib: Remove the rubbing cause; biopsy any patch that does not resolve

cards.head: Sun-damaged lips are a true precancer
cards.take: This review pooled 13 studies of 728 patients with actinic cheilitis, the sun damage of the lower lip seen in outdoor workers. Dryness and a blurred lip border were near universal; on biopsy, 34% had mild, 28% moderate and 15% severe dysplasia, and 14% turned malignant. Crusts, ulcers and red areas pointed to cancer. Chairside: advise lip sunscreen and biopsy any crusted or ulcerated area.
cards.rib: Advise lip sunscreen; biopsy crusts, ulcers or red patches

cards.head: Candida-infected white patches need follow-up too
cards.take: Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis is a firm white patch, often at the commissure, where Candida invades the surface layer. This review pooled nine studies and found that 12.1% of such lesions later became cancer, though study quality was mostly poor and diagnostic criteria varied. Chairside: treat the fungus and stop smoking first; if the patch persists after antifungals, biopsy and keep it under review.
cards.rib: Treat the Candida; biopsy the patch that persists after it

cards.ev: Cohort study · J Oral Pathol Med 2021
cards.head: DNA ploidy adds a little to dysplasia grade for risk
cards.take: This UK study followed 90 patients with oral potentially malignant lesions; 70 had usable DNA ploidy tests and 31 of them developed cancer. Severe dysplasia carried 3.5 times the risk of mild, and abnormal DNA content (aneuploidy) about twice the risk. Combining both predicted outcome only modestly. Chairside: if a report mentions aneuploidy, treat it as higher risk and refer for close review.
cards.rib: Treat an aneuploid report as high risk and refer promptly

cards.head: A visual exam misses about 3 in 10 risky lesions
cards.take: This review pooled 14 studies testing how well a conventional look-and-feel exam sorted visible oral lesions, against biopsy. For dysplasia or cancer, the exam picked up 71% and correctly cleared 85% of harmless lesions; for cancer alone, it caught 88%. Eyes alone miss many dysplastic lesions. Chairside: biopsy or refer persistent lesions in chewers and smokers rather than trusting their look.
cards.rib: Biopsy or refer persistent lesions instead of judging by eye

fig.title: Oral exam: share of lesions detected

cards.ev: Systematic review · J Evid Based Dent Pract 2024
cards.head: Rigorous fluoride is essential after head-neck radiation
cards.take: This review found five trials with 355 patients given up to 70 Gy of head and neck radiation. Caries rose by between 0.48 and 9.2 surfaces per year, and the biggest gap was between patients with rigorous and with poor fluoride use. Trials were small and flawed, but the effect looked large. Chairside: give daily high-fluoride gel or trays for life and recall often.
cards.rib: Prescribe daily high-fluoride gel for life after radiotherapy

fig.from: Luka, J Evid Based Dent Pract 2024

cards.head: Quitting tobacco cut new leukoplakia by about two-thirds
cards.take: In this 10-year Kerala study, 12,212 tobacco users were examined every year and counselled to quit. Among those who stopped, new leukoplakia appeared at about 0.31 times the rate seen in continuing users, and several other tobacco lesions almost vanished. Lichen planus showed no such link. Chairside: tell chewers and smokers that quitting now lowers their chance of developing a white patch.
cards.rib: Tell users quitting now lowers their chance of new white patches

cards.head: All-ceramic Maryland bridges: about 91% last 5 years
cards.take: This review pooled one RCT and seven cohort studies of all-ceramic resin-bonded bridges followed for at least 3 years. Estimated 5-year survival was 91.2%; debonding (12.2%) and framework fracture (4.8%) were the main problems. Single-retainer cantilever designs survived better and debonded and fractured less than two-retainer designs. Chairside: for a missing incisor, a one-wing bonded bridge is a sound, tooth-saving option.
cards.rib: Prefer one bonded wing over two for a single missing incisor

cards.head: Crown or filling after root canal? Evidence is thin
cards.take: Cochrane found just one trial: 117 root-filled premolars with fibre posts got either a metal-ceramic crown or a composite filling. At 3 years, no tooth was lost; restoration failures were 1 of 54 with crowns versus 3 of 53 with composites, a difference that could be chance. Evidence was very low quality. Chairside: decide by remaining tooth structure and patient needs, not by rule.
cards.rib: Judge each root-filled tooth by how much wall is left

cards.head: Partial dentures last well, but clasped teeth are at risk
cards.take: This meta-analysis pooled 46 studies of 4,359 removable partial dentures in 4,072 patients. Five-year survival was 95.1% for cast-clasp dentures and 91.7% for telescopic ones. Probing depth and mobility did not change, but gingival index rose a little. Abutment teeth were about twice as likely to be extracted, and non-vital teeth roughly three times. Chairside: protect and recall clasped teeth closely.
cards.rib: Check clasped and non-vital abutments at every recall visit

cards.head: Monolithic zirconia bridges chip far less than layered
cards.take: Shihabi and Chrcanovic pooled 74 studies with 6,370 tooth-supported zirconia bridges and crowns. Five-year survival was 93.3% for monolithic zirconia against 88.7% for porcelain-veneered zirconia. Minor chipping hit about 10.4% of veneered work versus 0.08% of monolithic. Abutments under veneered work also lost vitality more often (1.5% vs 0.3%). Chairside: for posterior bridges, choose monolithic zirconia where looks allow.
cards.rib: Choose monolithic zirconia for back-tooth bridges

cards.head: CBCT in endodontics only when a PA cannot answer
cards.take: The European Society of Endodontology says CBCT should follow a full clinical exam and conventional radiographs, and be used case by case when they leave the question open. Suitable cases include unclear periapical disease, trauma, complex anatomy, missed canals or perforation in retreatment, resorption, surgery planning and suspected root fracture. Chairside: justify it, use a field under 5 cm, and read the whole volume.
cards.rib: Take a periapical first; keep CBCT fields small and justified

fig.title: When ESE says CBCT may help

cards.head: AI spots periapical lesions well in early studies
cards.take: Pul and Schwendicke reviewed 24 studies of AI detecting periapical radiolucencies; four could be pooled. Pooled sensitivity was 94% and specificity 96%, but risk of bias was unclear to high, and most studies tested research models rather than commercial software in real clinics. Chairside: AI may be a useful second reader on periapicals, but your clinical tests and own reading still decide.
cards.rib: Use AI as a second reader; confirm with pulp tests

cards.head: CBCT finds more vertical root fractures than a PA
cards.take: This review included 23 studies, 16 pooled, comparing periapical films and CBCT for vertical root fractures. CBCT caught more fractures, with sensitivity of 70% against 51% for periapicals, while specificity was similar (84% vs 87%). Even CBCT missed nearly a third. Chairside: when a root fracture is suspected but the periapical is unclear, CBCT can help, though clinical signs still matter.
cards.rib: Suspect a root fracture? Add small-field CBCT if the PA is unclear

cards.head: Bitewing recall should follow caries risk, not habit
cards.take: The UK selection criteria guideline says routine x-rays without signs or symptoms cannot be justified. Bitewing intervals should follow each patient's caries risk: every six months for high-risk children and adults, yearly for moderate risk, and about every two years for low-risk adults and permanent dentitions. Panoramic views need specific clinical indications. Chairside: record caries risk, then set the bitewing interval.
cards.rib: Record caries risk first, then set the bitewing interval

fig.title: Recall bitewing interval by caries risk

cards.head: Loading implants right away fails no more than waiting
cards.take: This Cochrane review included 26 trials with 1,217 patients and 2,120 implants. Comparing immediate with conventional loading, it found no convincing difference in prosthesis or implant failure in the first year; bone loss differed by only 0.10 mm. Mean implant failure across trials was 2.5%. Evidence quality was low. Chairside: immediate loading suits well-selected cases with good primary stability.
cards.rib: Load immediately only when primary stability is high

cards.head: MTA is the best-supported pulpotomy agent for milk molars
cards.take: This Cochrane review pooled 87 small trials with 7,140 primary teeth. In pulpotomy, MTA cut clinical and radiological failure compared with formocresol (12 trials, moderate certainty) and also beat calcium hydroxide. Formocresol outperformed calcium hydroxide, but its toxicity argues for alternatives. Pulp treatment of milk teeth generally succeeds. Chairside: choose MTA for primary molar pulpotomy and avoid calcium hydroxide as the dressing.
cards.rib: Dress primary molar pulpotomies with MTA, not calcium hydroxide

cards.head: Oral midazolam helps anxious children cooperate
cards.take: This Cochrane review found 50 trials with 3,704 children testing 34 sedatives, with or without nitrous oxide; most trials were at high risk of bias. Only oral midazolam could be pooled: at 0.25 to 1 mg/kg it gave clearly more cooperative behaviour than placebo in 6 small studies (202 children; moderate certainty). Chairside: if trained and equipped, oral midazolam is the best-supported sedative choice.
cards.rib: Use oral midazolam only with sedation training and monitoring

cards.head: ART fillings in milk teeth fail more than drill-and-fill
cards.take: This Cochrane review included 15 trials with 3,760 people. In primary teeth restored with high-viscosity glass ionomer, hand-excavated ART restorations had higher odds of failure than conventional drilled ones over 12 to 24 months (OR 1.60; 5 studies, 643 children; low certainty). ART may hurt slightly less, but this is uncertain. Chairside: keep ART for outreach or very anxious children, and recall them closely.
cards.rib: Use ART where drills are impractical, and review it more often

cards.head: Coronectomy cuts nerve injury in high-risk wisdom teeth
cards.take: This meta-analysis pooled 42 observational studies with 3,095 patients whose lower third molars were at raised risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury. Compared with full extraction, coronectomy cut the odds of nerve injury sharply (OR 0.14) but raised the odds of needing a second operation (OR 5.38). Pain and dry socket did not clearly differ. Chairside: offer coronectomy when imaging shows close nerve contact.
cards.rib: Discuss coronectomy and possible reoperation before consent

cards.head: Articaine numbs more reliably than lidocaine
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials compared 4% articaine with 2% lidocaine for routine dental care. Articaine roughly doubled the odds of successful anaesthesia overall (OR 2.17), with the biggest gain for infiltrations (OR 2.78) and a smaller one for inferior alveolar blocks (OR 1.50). No trial reported major anaesthetic-related harms with either drug. Chairside: consider articaine infiltration, especially when lidocaine fails.
cards.rib: Reach for articaine infiltration when lidocaine falls short

fig.title: Odds of success, articaine vs lidocaine

cards.head: PRF in wisdom tooth sockets lowers dry socket risk
cards.take: This meta-analysis pooled 10 randomised trials with 314 patients having lower third molars removed. Placing platelet-rich fibrin in the socket cut dry socket risk by about two-thirds (RR 0.35) and modestly eased early pain, with a small swelling benefit; mouth opening was unchanged. No trial was at low risk of bias. Chairside: PRF is a reasonable add-on where a centrifuge is available, not a must.
cards.rib: Consider PRF for sockets at high risk of dry socket

cards.head: Painkillers clearly ease pain after brace adjustments
cards.take: This Cochrane review included 32 trials with 3,110 patients aged 9 to 34. Compared with placebo or nothing, analgesics lowered pain on a 100 mm scale by about 12 mm at 2 hours, 24 mm at 6 hours and 21 mm at 24 hours (moderate certainty). Ibuprofen-type drugs and paracetamol worked about the same. Chairside: advise a simple analgesic after placement and after each activation.
cards.rib: Tell patients paracetamol or ibuprofen both work after visits

fig.title: Pain cut vs placebo (100 mm scale)

cards.head: Vibration and laser add-ons don't shorten brace time
cards.take: This Cochrane review assessed 23 trials with 1,027 patients. Light vibration devices did not shorten overall treatment, reduce visits or speed alignment. Low-level laser and LED light shortened some early phases, such as alignment by about 50 days in 2 small trials, but none shortened total treatment and gains were of doubtful value. Certainty was low to very low. Chairside: don't sell accelerators as time-savers.
cards.rib: Tell patients gadgets will not cut their total treatment time

cards.head: Mini-screws save about 1.7 mm of molar anchorage
cards.take: This Cochrane review included 15 trials with 561 patients. Pooling 7 trials, surgical anchorage such as mini-screws reduced unwanted forward movement of upper first molars by 1.68 mm compared with conventional anchorage (moderate certainty), though results varied between trials. Total treatment time did not clearly differ, and no trial reported harms. Chairside: mini-screws are a sound choice when molar anchorage is critical.
cards.rib: Plan mini-screw anchorage for maximum-anchorage extraction cases

cards.head: Early acyclovir helps toddlers with herpetic gingivitis
cards.take: This Cochrane review found only two small trials. In the better one, 72 children under 6 with primary herpetic gingivostomatitis got acyclovir or placebo. After 8 days, acyclovir cut the risk of persisting mouth lesions by about 90% (RR 0.10) and eased eating and drinking problems; three placebo children needed hospital rehydration. Evidence is weak. Chairside: start acyclovir early and push fluids.
cards.rib: Start acyclovir early and keep the child well hydrated

lines: Mouth lesions at day 8 on drug

cards.head: Bad breath: no rinse, paste or gum is proven best
cards.take: This Cochrane review pooled 44 trials with 1809 adults testing tongue cleaning, mouthrinses, toothpastes, chewing gums, tablets and combinations for halitosis. Most followed people for only one to four weeks. Several options lowered odour scores slightly, but certainty was low to very low and no product or concentration beat the others. Chairside: look for the cause first, then teach daily tongue cleaning and good hygiene.
cards.rib: Look for the cause first, then teach daily tongue cleaning

cards.head: Oral thrush: most antifungals work, fluconazole ranks top
cards.take: This network meta-analysis of 31 trials and 4042 patients compared antifungals for oral candidiasis. Nine drugs, including nystatin, clotrimazole, miconazole gel and fluconazole, beat placebo for fungal cure. Fluconazole ranked highest (79%), just ahead of miconazole gel (77%), while nystatin ranked low (16%). Most trials carried high risk of bias. Chairside: an azole is a sound first choice; nystatin looks weaker.
cards.rib: Prefer an azole over nystatin when treating oral thrush

cards.head: Quitting smoking helps gums heal and slows bone loss
cards.take: Five studies followed patients for at least a year. In one 6-year study, attachment loss of 3 mm or more was about three times more common in continuing smokers than in quitters. Two long studies showed roughly 30% less bone loss in quitters, and quitters gained more pocket reduction after scaling. Evidence is limited. Chairside: build quit advice into every periodontal plan.
cards.rib: Add tobacco quit advice to every periodontal treatment plan

cards.head: For recession, a connective tissue graft edges ahead
cards.take: This Cochrane review covered 48 trials on recession of 3 mm or more. A connective tissue graft under a coronally advanced flap reduced recession 0.37 mm more than a membrane technique and gained about 1 to 1.8 mm more keratinised gum than enamel matrix or membranes. Most evidence was low quality. Chairside: graft when both root coverage and thicker gum matter; other techniques remain acceptable.
cards.rib: Use a connective tissue graft when thin gum also needs bulk

cards.head: A cold final rinse may ease pain after root canal work
cards.take: This meta-analysis of randomised trials (16 reviewed, 9 pooled) compared a cold final irrigant with a room-temperature one. Cold rinsing lowered pain scores by about 1.1 points at 6 and 24 hours, and by 0.4 to 0.7 points at 48 and 72 hours. Results varied widely and the evidence was low quality. Chairside: a cold saline final flush is cheap and simple to try.
cards.rib: Try a cold saline final flush to ease pain after the visit

fig.title: Pain score drop with cold final rinse

cards.head: Four factors decide whether a root canal heals
cards.take: This meta-analysis drew on 63 outcome studies of first-time root canal treatment to ask which clinical factors matter. Four improved success significantly: no periapical lesion before treatment, a root filling without voids, a filling ending within 2 mm of the radiographic apex, and a satisfactory coronal restoration. Studies varied a lot. Chairside: shape to the apex, fill densely without overfilling, and seal the crown well.
cards.rib: Fill densely to the apex, then place a sound coronal seal

fig.title: Factors linked to root canal success
rows: Filling within 2 mm of the apex

cards.head: Glass ionomer stays put better than composite in class V
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 13 clinical trials compared glass ionomer, conventional or resin-modified, with composite in non-carious cervical lesions over 12 to 36 months. Glass ionomer fillings were retained more often, by a risk difference of 7 percentage points. Colour, margins, surface texture, shape and secondary caries were similar. Chairside: for abrasion and abfraction lesions, consider glass ionomer when retention is the main worry.
cards.rib: Pick glass ionomer for cervical lesions where retention matters

cards.head: Universal adhesive in class V: etch first for retention
cards.take: This review of 20 trials (14 pooled) looked at universal adhesives in non-carious cervical lesions. Self-etch mode lost more fillings: etch-and-rinse cut the risk of retention loss by about 78% at 12 months and 68% at 18 to 24 months. Margins were similar, but self-etch caused less post-op sensitivity. Chairside: etch with phosphoric acid, at least selectively on enamel, for durable cervical fillings.
cards.rib: Phosphoric-etch the enamel margin before a universal adhesive

cards.head: COTPA: no tobacco sales to under-18s or near schools
cards.take: India's COTPA 2003 bans smoking in public places, hospital buildings included, and bans tobacco advertising. Selling tobacco to anyone under 18, or within 100 yards of an educational institution, is an offence with a fine of up to Rs 200. Packs must carry a pictorial warning covering 85% of the main display area. Chairside: keep your clinic smoke-free and use the pack warning when counselling.
cards.rib: Keep the clinic smoke-free and point to the pack warning

fig.title: Key COTPA 2003 rules
rows: No sale within 100 yards of schools

cards.head: Even after laser excision, dysplasia often comes back
cards.take: This UK cohort followed 100 patients for up to 10 years after laser excision of a single dysplastic oral lesion. 17 had same-site recurrence and 14 new lesions elsewhere; 5 turned malignant at the treated site and 2 developed cancer at new sites. 62 were disease-free at last review. Chairside: excision is not the end; keep reviewing the whole mouth for years.
cards.rib: Keep reviewing the whole mouth for years after excision

cards.head: Moderate dysplasia on a report is closer to severe
cards.take: This network meta-analysis of 41 studies (12,964 lesions) compared dysplasia grading on biopsy reports. Severe dysplasia carried 4.42 times the odds of malignant transformation of mild dysplasia, and moderate dysplasia 2.66 times, closer to severe than to mild. The binary high/low grade system was simpler but hid this middle group. Chairside: treat a moderate dysplasia report as high risk and refer for management.
cards.rib: Treat a moderate dysplasia report as high risk and refer

fig.title: Odds of malignant change vs mild dysplasia

cards.head: Plain supari is not safe: it raises oral cancer risk too
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 50 publications found that, on the Indian subcontinent, chewing betel quid or areca nut without tobacco raised the risk of oral and oropharyngeal cancer about 2.5-fold (RR 2.56), and betel quid with tobacco about 7.7-fold (RR 7.74). Risk climbed with the amount and years of chewing, independent of smoking and alcohol. Chairside: advise stopping supari and paan masala, not just gutkha.
cards.rib: Advise quitting supari and paan masala, not only gutkha

cards.head: Quitting chewing lowers head and neck cancer risk
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 13 studies, mostly Asian, found that former users of smokeless tobacco and betel quid had lower head and neck cancer risk than current users: 0.73 for areca nut without tobacco and 0.66 for betel quid with tobacco. After 20 or more years of quitting, risk fell to 0.37. Chairside: tell long-time chewers it is never too late; quitting today still pays off.
cards.rib: Tell long-time chewers that quitting now still lowers their risk

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · J Prosthet Dent 2016
cards.head: Implants in irradiated jaws mostly survive, but less well
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 40 studies (2220 patients, 9231 implants) found an 84.3% survival rate for implants placed in irradiated jaw bone, significantly lower than in non-irradiated bone. Close monitoring was needed to limit complications such as osteoradionecrosis. Chairside: implants can restore function after head and neck radiotherapy, but plan them with the oncology team and keep these patients on tight recall.
cards.rib: Plan implants after radiotherapy with the oncology team

cards.head: Jaw-stretching devices help trismus after cancer care
cards.take: This review of 32 studies found that force-applying jaw devices improved mouth opening in established trismus after head and neck cancer treatment: a mean gain of 9.5 mm versus 2.4 mm in controls. Preventive use did not improve opening, and 8 adverse events, including jaw and molar fractures, were reported. Chairside: measure mouth opening at every recall and refer early for supervised jaw rehabilitation.
cards.rib: Measure mouth opening at each recall and refer early for rehab

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · Front Oral Health 2024
cards.head: AI reading mouth images is promising, not a diagnosis
cards.take: This review of 55 studies, with a pooled meta-analysis, found that AI algorithms reading clinical images of the mouth detected oral cancer and potentially malignant disorders with 87% sensitivity and 81% specificity. Most models were tested on curated datasets, not in busy clinics. Chairside: an AI flag can prompt a closer look or referral, but a suspicious lesion still needs a specialist opinion and biopsy.
cards.rib: Use AI as a prompt to refer, never as a reason to skip biopsy

fig.title: AI on oral images: pooled accuracy

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · J Oral Pathol Med 2018
cards.head: 1 in 10 Asians may carry a potentially malignant lesion
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 22 population studies put the worldwide prevalence of oral potentially malignant disorders at 4.47%, rising to 10.54% in Asia, the highest of any region. About 60% of affected people were men. In a busy Indian practice that means several such patients every week, most unaware. Chairside: examine every mucosal surface at every new-patient visit, not only the tooth that hurts.
cards.rib: Examine all mucosal surfaces at every new-patient visit

cards.head: India's free text-message quit service helps some users
cards.take: A telephone survey of 3362 tobacco users registered with India's government mCessation text-message programme found that, 4 to 6 months after joining, 19% reported no tobacco use in the past 30 days and 66% of those still using had tried to quit. Quitting was self-reported and there was no control group. Chairside: alongside your advice, help chewers sign up for the free national quit service.
cards.rib: Help each tobacco user enrol in the free national quit service

cards.head: Rubber dam may help fillings last longer
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 6 trials (1342 people, mostly children) compared rubber dam with cotton rolls. Cervical composites placed under rubber dam were more likely to survive at 6 months (OR 2.29), and in one large trial of ART fillings in primary molars rubber dam lowered 2-year failure (HR 0.80). All trials had high risk of bias. Chairside: use rubber dam when moisture control matters.
cards.rib: Use rubber dam whenever moisture control decides the result

cards.head: Resin sealants on molars prevent most occlusal caries
cards.take: This Cochrane review found that resin sealants on permanent molars of children aged 5 to 10 sharply cut occlusal decay at 2 years (OR 0.12, moderate certainty), with benefit still seen at 4 years. Where 40% of unsealed molars decayed, only about 6% of sealed molars did. Many trials were old. Chairside: seal first molars soon after eruption in at-risk children and check retention.
cards.rib: Seal erupting first molars and check sealant retention at recall

cards.head: Use a toothpaste with at least 1000 ppm fluoride
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 96 trials found that fluoride toothpaste prevents decay compared with non-fluoride paste, with high-certainty evidence for 1000-1250 ppm in children's permanent teeth, and stronger pastes (1450-1500 ppm) preventing a little more. Low-fluoride pastes did worse in some comparisons. In young children, weigh strength against fluorosis risk by using a smear or pea-sized amount. Chairside: check the ppm on the family's tube.
cards.rib: Check the ppm on the tube, and teach a smear or pea-sized amount

fig.title: Fluoride paste vs non-fluoride, permanent teeth

cards.head: A preoperative antibiotic dose cuts early implant loss
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 14 studies, including 8 randomised trials, found that prophylactic antibiotics at implant placement lowered implant failure (RR 0.55). About 50 patients need to be treated to prevent one failure. Antibiotics did not reduce postoperative infections in healthy patients, and the result held when high-bias studies were excluded. Chairside: weigh a prophylactic dose against antibiotic stewardship for each patient.
cards.rib: Weigh implant prophylaxis against antibiotic stewardship

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · Matern Child Health J 2022
cards.head: Gum disease in pregnancy is linked to preeclampsia
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 30 observational studies (6 cohort, 24 case-control) found that pregnant women with periodontitis had about three times the odds of preeclampsia (OR 3.18), and higher odds in lower-middle-income countries (OR 6.70). These studies show an association, not proof that periodontal treatment prevents preeclampsia. Chairside: screen expectant mothers' gums and do not ignore periodontitis during pregnancy.
cards.rib: Screen pregnant patients' gums and don't ignore periodontitis

cards.head: Sleeping in dentures doubles pneumonia risk in the old
cards.take: This Japanese cohort followed 524 adults aged 85 or over for 3 years. Of 453 denture wearers, 40.8% kept their dentures in overnight, and they had more than twice the risk of pneumonia-related hospitalisation or death (HR 2.38). They also had more tongue and denture plaque and gum inflammation. Chairside: tell every elderly denture wearer and carer to remove and clean the denture at night.
cards.rib: Tell elderly patients and carers to take dentures out at night

cards.head: Digital complete dentures save chair time and fit well
cards.take: This review of 73 studies compared CAD-CAM (milled or 3D-printed) complete dentures with conventional ones. CAD-CAM dentures needed less chairside time, cost less overall and retained better; milled bases were stronger and smoother, while conventional dentures still looked better than printed ones. A digital record also makes a lost denture easy to remake. Chairside: digital dentures are a sound option for edentulous patients where available.
cards.rib: Consider digital dentures and keep the file for easy remakes

cards.head: Powered toothbrushes remove a little more plaque
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 51 trials (4624 people) found powered toothbrushes reduced plaque by 11% at 1-3 months and by 21% after 3 months compared with manual brushes, and gingivitis by 6% and 11%, with moderate-certainty evidence. The clinical importance of these differences is unclear. Chairside: technique and twice-daily habit matter most; suggest a powered brush for patients with limited dexterity or poor results.
cards.rib: Teach technique first; suggest a powered brush for poor dexterity

fig.title: Reduction vs manual brush, over 3 months

cards.head: Extract on blood thinners without stopping most drugs
cards.take: The 2022 SDCEP guidance advises treating patients on aspirin without stopping it, and treating warfarin patients without interruption if the INR, checked ideally within 24 hours, is below 4. For higher-risk procedures on apixaban or dabigatran, the morning dose is missed; rivaroxaban or edoxaban morning doses wait until 4 hours after haemostasis. Chairside: work early in the day, limit the area, and suture and pack.
cards.rib: Don't stop anticoagulants yourself; use local haemostasis well

cards.head: Healthy impacted wisdom teeth need not be removed
cards.take: NICE guidance advises against removing impacted third molars that show no disease. Removal should be kept for clear pathology: unrestorable caries, untreatable pulp or periapical infection, cellulitis or abscess, resorption, fracture, cysts or tumours, or teeth in the way of other surgery. A first episode of pericoronitis is not an indication unless severe; a second or later episode is. Chairside: monitor symptom-free impacted teeth instead.
cards.rib: Watch symptom-free impacted molars; remove only for clear disease

fig.title: NICE: when to remove a wisdom tooth

cards.head: Ibuprofen before the block helps a hot pulp go numb
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 7 trials found that taking ibuprofen before treatment raised the success of the inferior alveolar nerve block in irreversible pulpitis (RR 1.79 overall; RR 1.55 in symptomatic cases) and lowered pain during treatment. The evidence came from small trials. Chairside: if the patient has no contraindication, give ibuprofen before the appointment, and keep supplemental injections ready.
cards.rib: Give ibuprofen before the block if there is no contraindication

cards.head: Cold sores: tablets prevent a few, creams do not
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 32 trials (2640 people) found that long-term oral antivirals such as aciclovir or valaciclovir reduced herpes labialis recurrences, but the benefit was small. Short-term aciclovir 400 mg twice daily lowered recurrence in two small trials (RR 0.26), while aciclovir cream did not prevent outbreaks (RR 0.91), nor did lysine. Chairside: for frequent recurrences, discuss antiviral prophylaxis with the patient's doctor.
cards.rib: Discuss oral antiviral prophylaxis for frequent cold sores

cards.head: Burning mouth syndrome: no treatment is proven yet
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 23 placebo-controlled trials (1121 participants, 83% women) found only very low-certainty evidence for any treatment of burning mouth syndrome. Topical clonazepam, electromagnetic therapy and psychological therapy each showed some relief in small single trials; alpha lipoic acid caused more headaches and stomach upset. Chairside: first exclude local and systemic causes of burning, then explain the condition and refer to oral medicine.
cards.rib: Exclude other causes first, then refer to an oral physician

cards.head: High-fluoride paste may cut white spots during braces
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 10 trials (1798 patients) found low-certainty evidence that 5000 ppm fluoride toothpaste reduced new white spot lesions during fixed appliance treatment compared with 1450 ppm paste (18% vs 27%), and that professionally applied fluoride foam also helped in one small trial. Varnish every six weeks showed no clear benefit. Chairside: prescribe high-fluoride paste for brace wearers with poor plaque control.
cards.rib: Prescribe high-fluoride paste to brace wearers with poor hygiene

fig.title: New white spot lesions during braces

cards.head: Quad-helix beats a removable plate for crossbite
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 31 trials (about 1410 patients) found that in children aged 7 to 11, a fixed quad-helix corrected posterior crossbites more often than a removable expansion plate (RR 1.29, moderate certainty), and worked faster. In adolescents, different rapid maxillary expanders performed similarly. Chairside: spot a unilateral crossbite with a functional shift early in the mixed dentition and refer for fixed expansion.
cards.rib: Spot crossbites early in mixed dentition and refer for expansion

cards.ev: Report · WHO Global Oral Health Status Report 2022
cards.head: Oral disease affects 3.5 billion people, WHO says
cards.take: WHO's 2022 global report estimated that oral diseases affect about 45% of the world's population, 3.5 billion people, three in four of them in low- and middle-income countries. Untreated caries affects about 2.5 billion, severe gum disease about 1 billion, and oral cancer adds about 380,000 new cases a year. WHO urges oral care within primary care. Chairside: prevention advice counts.
cards.rib: Give sugar, tobacco and fluoride advice to every patient

cards.head: Indian dental prescriptions are heavy on antibiotics
cards.take: This review of 50 Indian studies found antibiotics made up 27% to 88% of all dental prescriptions, most studies reporting over half. Many were fixed-dose combinations, some not recommended by WHO's AWaRe list, and 5% to 35% of patients self-medicated with antibiotics for dental problems. Study quality was low to moderate. Chairside: treat the source of infection first and avoid combination antibiotics.
cards.rib: Treat the source first; save antibiotics for spreading infection

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · J Clin Periodontol 2015
cards.head: Peri-implant mucositis: cleaning works, add-ons don't
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 7 studies (140 patients) found that adding antiseptics, antibiotics or an air-abrasive device to professional plaque removal did not significantly improve bleeding on probing, gingival index or pocket depth in peri-implant mucositis. Complete resolution was uncommon with any protocol. Chairside: treat bleeding around implants early with thorough mechanical cleaning and better home care, and recall these patients regularly.
cards.rib: Clean bleeding implants mechanically and recall regularly

cards.head: Implants without keratinised gum get peri-implantitis more
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 22 studies (4044 patients, 13,265 implants) found that implants lacking keratinised mucosa had nearly three times the odds of peri-implantitis (OR 2.78); with a 2 mm cut-off the OR was 2.73. The risk persisted in patients on regular maintenance. Most studies were cross-sectional; certainty was moderate. Chairside: check keratinised tissue before placement and consider grafting when there is under 2 mm.
cards.rib: Check keratinised tissue width before and after implant placement

cards.head: X-rays miss about half of early caries lesions
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 77 studies (15,518 tooth surfaces) found dental imaging detected early caries with a pooled sensitivity of only 0.47 but good specificity of 0.88. In 1000 surfaces, about 337 early lesions would be missed. CBCT did not justify its dose for caries detection. Certainty was low. Chairside: combine radiographs with careful visual-tactile examination and manage early lesions with prevention.
cards.rib: Pair bitewings with a careful visual exam; prevent, don't drill

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · Clin Oral Investig 2019
cards.head: Bulk-fill composites perform like layered ones
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 10 clinical studies (941 posterior restorations, mean follow-up 33.6 months) found no significant difference in failure between conventional layered composites and either flowable base bulk-fill (RR 1.49) or sculptable full-body bulk-fill (RR 1.89) materials. Longer trials are still needed. Chairside: bulk-fill can save time in posterior cavities, provided you respect the maker's increment depth and curing time.
cards.rib: Respect bulk-fill depth limits and curing time to save chair time

cards.head: Many caries lesions can be stopped without a drill
cards.take: This network meta-analysis behind the ADA guideline pooled 44 trials (7378 participants) on 22 non-restorative caries treatments. For non-cavitated occlusal lesions, sealants plus 5% NaF varnish ranked among the best; for non-cavitated approximal lesions, resin infiltration plus varnish. Twice-yearly 38% SDF best arrested cavitated coronal lesions, and 5000 ppm paste root lesions. Chairside: match the non-invasive option to the lesion before drilling.
cards.rib: Match a non-invasive option to each lesion before you drill

cards.head: Splints for jaw pain: evidence is still very uncertain
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 57 trials (2846 people) on occlusal interventions for temporomandibular disorders found only very low-certainty evidence. A hard stabilisation splint may reduce muscle pain on chewing compared with no treatment, but compared with placebo splints, painkillers, physiotherapy or acupuncture there was little or no clear difference. Chairside: start with explanation, self-care and simple exercises; avoid irreversible occlusal grinding for TMD.
cards.rib: Start TMD care with reassurance, self-care and reversible options

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · J Clin Periodontol 2020 (EFP)
cards.head: Antibiotics with deep scaling add only about 0.5 mm
cards.take: This EFP workshop meta-analysis of 28 studies found that systemic antibiotics added to subgingival instrumentation gave statistically significant but modest extra pocket reduction: about 0.45 mm short term and 0.49 mm long term. Amoxicillin plus metronidazole performed best (0.54 mm at 12 months), but adverse events were more frequent. Chairside: do thorough instrumentation first, and reserve adjunctive antibiotics for selected severe cases.
cards.rib: Instrument thoroughly; keep antibiotics for selected severe cases

cards.head: Parotid-sparing radiotherapy halves severe dry mouth
cards.take: In the UK PARSPORT trial, 94 patients with pharyngeal cancer were randomised to conventional radiotherapy or parotid-sparing intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT). At 12 months, significant dry mouth affected 74% versus 38%, and at 24 months 83% versus 29%, with better saliva recovery and no loss of cancer control. Chairside: ask which radiotherapy your patient had, since dry mouth after older techniques needs especially close caries prevention.
cards.rib: Ask how the patient was irradiated, and plan caries prevention

cards.head: Indian dentists are well placed to screen high-risk mouths
cards.take: This review in JCO Global Oncology, built on a systematic search plus GLOBOCAN and government data, argues that opportunistic screening of high-risk groups by dentists, using a simple visual oral examination at routine visits, is a cost-effective way to catch potentially malignant disorders in India. Studies abroad show it is feasible; none had been reported from India. Chairside: examine every chewer's mucosa.
cards.rib: Examine and record the mucosa of every tobacco or areca user

cards.ev: Cross-sectional study · J Family Community Med 2013
cards.head: Fissured tongue and lingual varices are common variants
cards.take: In a North Indian dental outpatient survey of 8866 adults, fissured tongue was seen in 3.3% and lingual varices in 2.73%, and the tongue was the site of 64.4% of all mucosal variants recorded. Both are harmless. Food can collect in deep fissures and cause soreness. Chairside: reassure, advise gentle tongue brushing, and reserve concern for a fissure that ulcerates, hardens or bleeds.
cards.rib: Reassure about fissures; worry only if one ulcerates or hardens

cards.head: Deep caries: stop short of the pulp, fail less often
cards.take: A Cochrane network meta-analysis pooled 27 trials (3350 people, 4195 teeth). In deep lesions of permanent teeth, complete removal to hard dentine failed more often than stepwise excavation (OR 2.06) and far more than selective removal leaving soft dentine over the pulp (OR 11.32, wide CI). Most trials had high risk of bias. Chairside: clear the periphery fully, leave leathery dentine pulpally, seal well.
cards.rib: Leave soft dentine over the pulp, but seal the margins well

fig.title: Deep lesions, permanent teeth: odds of failure

cards.head: Posterior composites fail about twice as often as amalgam
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 8 trials (mostly children) found composite fillings in back teeth failed more often than amalgam (RR 1.89) and developed more secondary caries (RR 2.14); fracture rates were similar. Evidence certainty was low and the trials are old. Chairside: if you place posterior composites, isolate well and manage caries risk, and discuss longevity honestly with the patient.
cards.rib: Isolate well and control caries risk when placing composites

cards.head: Fluoride varnish cuts caries by about 40% in children
cards.take: This Cochrane review pooled 22 trials with 12,455 children. Fluoride varnish applied two to four times a year reduced decayed, missing and filled surfaces by 43% in permanent teeth and by 37% in primary teeth compared with placebo or no treatment. Evidence quality was moderate. Chairside: varnish takes a minute, needs no special cooperation and suits every child at raised caries risk.
cards.rib: Apply fluoride varnish 2-4 times a year in at-risk children

cards.head: Hall crowns beat usual fillings in primary molars
cards.take: In a Scottish practice-based trial of 132 children, one carious primary molar got a preformed metal crown cemented without drilling or local anaesthetic (Hall technique) and the other got the dentist's usual filling. At 5 years, major failures (pain, abscess, pulpitis) were 3% with Hall crowns versus 16.5% with fillings. Chairside: for an asymptomatic carious primary molar, Hall crowns are a quick, well-tolerated option.
cards.rib: Seal asymptomatic carious primary molars under a Hall crown

cards.ev: Network meta-analysis · J Oral Pathol Med 2023
cards.head: Aphthous ulcers: no topical gel clearly wins on pain
cards.take: A network meta-analysis compared 20 topical medicines for recurrent aphthous stomatitis across 43 randomised trials (3067 people). None was clearly better than the others for pain, with low-to-moderate certainty evidence; topical doxycycline ranked best for speeding healing. Chairside: choose a cheap, safe topical, start it early in the ulcer cycle, and look for triggers such as trauma, deficiency or systemic disease in frequent cases.
cards.rib: Start a simple topical early and look for causes in frequent cases

cards.head: Denture stomatitis: topical antifungal plus denture care
cards.take: A network meta-analysis of 25 studies ranked treatments for denture stomatitis. Topical antifungals gave the most clinical improvement (RR 4.37 vs control), and microwave disinfection of the denture plus a topical antifungal gave the best Candida clearance (RR 7.38). Confidence in the evidence was low. Chairside: prescribe a topical antifungal and treat the denture too, with nightly removal and cleaning.
cards.rib: Treat the denture as well as the palate, and remove it at night

cards.head: Routine CBCT before third molar removal adds little
cards.take: In a multicentre trial, 256 patients having lower wisdom teeth removed were randomised to planning with CBCT or a panoramic radiograph. Nerve numbness at 7 days was 1.5% after CBCT and 3.8% after panoramic planning, a difference that was not significant, and CBCT did not reduce complications. Chairside: start with a good OPG; keep CBCT for cases where the root clearly overlaps the canal.
cards.rib: Start with an OPG; keep CBCT for close root-canal relations

cards.head: AI on bitewings helps dentists spot more caries
cards.take: In a randomised crossover trial, 22 dentists read bitewing radiographs with or without an AI caries-detection aid. With AI, sensitivity rose from 0.72 to 0.81 and overall accuracy (AUC) from 0.85 to 0.89, with no significant loss of specificity. But dentists using AI also chose more invasive treatment. Chairside: treat AI marks as a second opinion; an enamel shadow still deserves prevention, not a drill.
cards.rib: Use AI marks as a second look; keep enamel lesions non-invasive

cards.head: Rectangular collimation cuts intraoral X-ray dose sharply
cards.take: A systematic review of 13 studies found that switching from a round to a rectangular collimator reduced patient radiation dose by 40% to 92% for intraoral radiographs, with moderate-quality evidence. Retakes may rise briefly while staff learn to align it. Chairside: fit a rectangular collimator on every intraoral unit, use holders for alignment and the fastest receptor, especially for children.
cards.rib: Fit a rectangular collimator and use film holders for alignment

cards.head: Lead aprons and thyroid collars no longer advised
cards.take: The American Academy of Oral and Maxillofacial Radiology reviewed dose studies and advised stopping gonadal, pelvic and fetal shielding for all dental radiographs, and not using thyroid collars for intraoral, panoramic, cephalometric or CBCT imaging. Modern beams expose these organs very little, and shields can block the view and cause retakes. Chairside: protect patients through justified images, rectangular collimation and fast receptors instead.
cards.rib: Protect with justification, collimation and fast receptors instead

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · Int J Prosthodont 2026
cards.head: Monolithic ceramic crowns now match metal-ceramic
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 64 studies (over 11,500 single crowns) found 5-year survival of 98.5% for monolithic lithium disilicate, 96.8% for monolithic zirconia and 97.1% for metal-ceramic crowns. Feldspathic ceramic crowns did worst at 90.4%. Monolithic designs reduced chipping and fracture. Chairside: for a single crown, a monolithic lithium disilicate or zirconia crown is a reliable metal-free choice.
cards.rib: Choose a monolithic design to avoid veneer chipping

cards.head: Lost molars: shortened arch does as well as a partial
cards.take: In a German multicentre trial, 152 patients missing all molars in one jaw got either a partial denture replacing the molars or a shortened dental arch ending at the premolars. After 5 years, survival free of further tooth loss was 0.74 in both groups. Chairside: when premolars are sound, a shortened arch is a valid, cheaper plan without a denture.
cards.rib: Offer a shortened arch when premolars are healthy and stable

cards.head: Scaling and root planing lowers HbA1c in diabetes
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 35 trials (3249 people with diabetes and periodontitis) found that subgingival instrumentation lowered HbA1c by 0.43 percentage points at 3-4 months and by 0.30 at 6 months compared with no treatment or usual care. The evidence was moderate certainty and further trials are unlikely to change it. Chairside: treat diabetic patients' periodontitis and tell their physician it helps.
cards.rib: Screen diabetic patients' gums and treat periodontitis early

cards.ev: Population attributable fraction study · Lancet Oncol 2024
cards.head: One in three oral cancers comes from chewing
cards.take: IARC researchers estimated that over 120,000 oral cancers worldwide in 2022, one third of all cases, were caused by smokeless tobacco and areca nut. India alone accounted for 83,400 of them and Bangladesh for 9,700; 77% were in men. Areca nut itself is largely unregulated. Chairside: ask every patient about gutkha, khaini, paan and plain supari, and record it like a vital sign.
cards.rib: Ask every patient about tobacco, paan and plain supari use

cards.head: Dentists can help patients quit tobacco
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 20 trials (14,897 people) tested quit support given in dental settings. Even a single session of behavioural support roughly doubled long-term abstinence (RR 1.86, very low certainty). Support plus nicotine replacement raised quit rates to 74 per 1000, against 27 per 1000 without support (moderate certainty). Chairside: ask, advise and offer help at every visit, and add nicotine replacement for smokers.
cards.rib: Ask, advise and offer quit help at every single visit

cards.head: Stains and lights cannot replace a biopsy
cards.take: This Cochrane review pooled 63 studies of 7942 suspicious mouth lesions. Vital staining (such as toluidine blue) caught 86% of cancers and dysplasias but was specific only 68% of the time; light-based devices 87% and 50%. Brush cytology did best at 90% and 94%. No adjunct can replace a scalpel biopsy. Chairside: a suspicious lesion goes for biopsy, whatever a stain or light shows.
cards.rib: Biopsy every suspicious lesion, whatever the stain or light shows

cards.head: No pill or gel is proven to stop leukoplakia turning
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 14 trials (909 people) tested vitamin A, beta carotene, lycopene, bleomycin and other treatments for oral leukoplakia. Some healed lesions for a while, but relapse was common and none reduced cancer risk compared with placebo over 2 to 7 years. No trial has tested surgery against no treatment. Chairside: rely on biopsy, habit cessation and lifelong review, not on supplements.
cards.rib: Rely on biopsy, habit cessation and review, not supplements

cards.head: Irradiated jaw: save the tooth, and plan any extraction
cards.take: The 2024 ISOO-MASCC-ASCO guideline flags jaw doses of 50 Gy or more as the osteoradionecrosis risk zone. After radiotherapy, prefer root canal treatment, fillings or crowns over extraction in high-risk areas. If extraction is unavoidable, check the radiation plan, consider antibiotics and pentoxifylline-tocopherol, and use chlorhexidine rinses. Daily prescription fluoride (strong recommendation) prevents the caries that lead to extractions.
cards.rib: Check the jaw dose map before extracting after radiotherapy

cards.head: Low-level laser helps prevent radiation mouth sores
cards.take: The MASCC/ISOO systematic review and guideline recommends intraoral photobiomodulation (low-level laser) to prevent oral mucositis and its pain in head and neck radiotherapy, with or without chemotherapy, and in stem cell transplant. Benefit depends on following a tested protocol exactly, for example 632.8 nm at 3 J/cm2, five days a week through radiotherapy. Chairside: if you have a suitable laser, coordinate with the oncology team.
cards.rib: Offer protocol-based laser therapy during head-neck radiotherapy

cards.ev: WHO Collaborating Centre consensus · Oral Dis 2021
cards.head: WHO's 2020 list of potentially malignant disorders
cards.take: An international WHO Collaborating Centre seminar updated the list of oral potentially malignant disorders. Most entities stayed. Oral lichenoid lesions and oral chronic graft-versus-host disease were added; chronic hyperplastic candidosis and verrucous hyperplasia were dropped for lack of evidence, and epidermolysis bullosa was moved to limited evidence. Chairside: a lichenoid lesion next to a restoration or drug history also needs follow-up.
cards.rib: Keep lichenoid lesions on your recall list, not just leukoplakia

cards.head: Trained health workers can spot oral lesions well
cards.take: This meta-analysis pooled 5 studies with 10,069 people screened by trained frontline health workers using a simple visual mouth examination. They picked up oral cancers and potentially malignant disorders with 88.8% sensitivity and 91.9% specificity. No eligible studies tested stains, cytology or lights for mass screening. Chairside: a careful look with good light, done by a trained person, is the screening tool that works.
cards.rib: Train your staff to look, and refer every positive screen

cards.head: Phone photos plus a remote specialist catch most lesions
cards.take: In an Indian multicentre study, 5025 people were screened by frontline workers who photographed the mouth with a phone-based device. Remote specialists reading the images agreed with on-site specialists with 95% sensitivity and 84% specificity, whereas workers judging by eye alone reached only 60% sensitivity. Chairside: clear intraoral photos sent to an oral specialist are a reliable way to triage a doubtful lesion.
cards.rib: Send clear intraoral photos to a specialist when unsure

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · Front Public Health 2023
cards.head: Oral cancer patients wait about 7 weeks before seeking help
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 28 studies (30,845 patients) timed each step of the oral cancer pathway. The median wait from first symptom to first visit was 47 days, then 35 days from first visit to diagnosis and 30 days from diagnosis to treatment. Longer waits were shaped by social and economic context and may worsen survival. Chairside: arrange biopsy or referral that week.
cards.rib: Book the biopsy or referral the same week you see the lesion

fig.title: Median intervals on the oral cancer pathway

cards.head: Helping gutkha and khaini users quit: what works
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 34 trials (over 16,000 smokeless tobacco users) found varenicline raised quit rates (RR 1.34), as did nicotine lozenges (RR 1.36, low confidence). Nicotine patches, gum and bupropion showed no clear benefit. Most behavioural programmes helped, though effect sizes varied. Chairside: give clear quit advice and a follow-up date, and refer heavy chewers to a cessation clinic for medication.
cards.rib: Advise quitting, set a date and refer heavy chewers for medicine

cards.head: Floss or interdental brushes add a little to brushing
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 35 trials (3929 adults) found that adding floss or interdental brushes to toothbrushing may reduce gingivitis and plaque in the short term, and interdental brushes may work better than floss. Evidence for wooden sticks and water flossers was limited and inconsistent; certainty was low to very low. Chairside: size and demonstrate an interdental brush for open spaces; floss tight contacts.
cards.rib: Size and demonstrate an interdental brush for open contacts

cards.head: Full pulpotomy matches root canal in painful vital molars
cards.take: In a randomised trial of 160 mature molars with irreversible pulpitis, full pulpotomy with a calcium silicate cement was compared with root canal treatment. At 12 months clinical success was 97.3% vs 98.6% and radiographic success 93.3% vs 94.6%, while pain fell faster on day 1 after pulpotomy. Follow-up is short. Chairside: when bleeding stops after pulp removal, full pulpotomy is a quicker, cheaper option.
cards.rib: Offer full pulpotomy when coronal pulp bleeding can be controlled

cards.head: No retainer type is clearly best after braces
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 47 studies (4377 patients) compared fixed and removable retainers. Differences in lower incisor alignment were under 1 mm, too small to matter clinically. Clear plastic retainers failed less often than Hawley retainers (RR 0.60) and were more comfortable. Evidence was low to very low certainty. Chairside: pick a retainer the patient will actually wear, and plan long-term retention checks.
cards.rib: Choose the retainer the patient will wear, and review it yearly

cards.ev: Systematic review of RCTs · Int J Oral Implantol 2019
cards.head: Short implants can spare the posterior mandible a graft
cards.take: This review pooled 4 randomised trials (135 patients) comparing short implants with longer implants placed after vertical bone augmentation in atrophic posterior mandibles. At 5 years implant and prosthesis failures were similar, but the graft route had far more complications (RR 4.72) and 0.6 mm more bone loss. Chairside: with limited height above the canal, consider short implants before referring for vertical augmentation.
cards.rib: Consider short implants before planning a vertical bone graft

cards.head: Smokers' implants fail more than twice as often
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 292 publications covered over 150,000 implants. Implants in smokers had 2.4 times the odds of failure of those in non-smokers (OR 2.402), in both jaws, and lost 0.58 mm more marginal bone. The effect did not fade with longer follow-up. Most studies were retrospective. Chairside: document smoking before implant planning, warn about the risk, and offer quit support well before surgery.
cards.rib: Record smoking and offer quit support before planning implants

cards.head: Chlorhexidine roughly halves dry socket risk
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 49 trials found that chlorhexidine rinse (0.12% or 0.2%) or 0.2% chlorhexidine gel placed in the socket probably reduces dry socket, with odds ratios of 0.38 and 0.44 (moderate certainty). Benefit depends on baseline risk: about 7 surgical third molars treated prevent one dry socket, but 162 simple extractions. Chairside: use chlorhexidine for surgical third molars and other high-risk extractions.
cards.rib: Use chlorhexidine around surgical third molar removal

fig.title: Number needed to treat to prevent one dry socket

cards.ev: Systematic review & meta-analysis · Int J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2019
cards.head: Submucosal dexamethasone eases pain and swelling
cards.take: This meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials found that a submucosal dexamethasone injection at lower third molar surgery reduced early pain and swelling: about 4 patients treated spares one from early pain, and 5 from early oedema. The effect on mouth opening was under 5 mm and not clinically important. Evidence was low to moderate quality. Chairside: consider submucosal dexamethasone for difficult surgical third molars.
cards.rib: Consider submucosal dexamethasone for difficult third molars

fig.title: Submucosal dexamethasone: number needed to treat

cards.head: About 1 in 8 children has molar-incisor hypomineralisation
cards.take: Pooling 116 studies, this meta-analysis put the global prevalence of molar-incisor hypomineralisation (MIH) at 13.5%, and 10.7% in Asia. Affected first molars are often sensitive, break down quickly and are hard to anaesthetise. Chairside: check every first permanent molar and incisor at age 6 to 8 for chalky or yellow-brown patches, start fluoride and sealants early, and recall more often.
cards.rib: Check first molars at age 6-8 for chalky, sensitive patches

cards.head: One visit or two: root canal healing is the same
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 47 trials (5805 patients) found no difference in radiological failure at a year or more between single-visit and multiple-visit root canal treatment (RR 0.93, moderate certainty), and no clear difference in swelling, flare-ups or extractions. Single-visit patients more often reported pain within the first week (RR 1.55). Chairside: choose by time, isolation and canal control, and warn about soreness.
cards.rib: Pick visits by case control, and warn of first-week soreness

cards.head: Sensitive teeth: most desensitising pastes beat fluoride
cards.take: This network meta-analysis of 125 trials (12,541 patients) ranked desensitising toothpastes for dentine hypersensitivity. Calcium sodium phosphosilicate was most beneficial across touch, cold and air stimuli with moderate to high certainty; stannous fluoride, potassium, arginine and strontium pastes also beat regular fluoride. Chairside: rule out caries and cracks, then advise twice-daily use of a desensitising paste for several weeks.
cards.rib: Rule out caries and cracks, then prescribe a desensitising paste

cards.head: Repaired composites last as long as replaced ones
cards.take: This Dutch practice-based study followed 8542 composite restorations in 3239 patients. Failing restorations were either repaired (616) or replaced (264). Ten-year success was 43.4% after repair and 48.6% after replacement, and the authors concluded that repairs last as long as replacements while increasing overall survival. Chairside: for a chipped or partly failed composite, repair first instead of drilling it all out.
cards.rib: Repair a partly failed composite before replacing it

cards.head: Only 1 in 3 Indian chewers is advised to quit
cards.take: India's second Global Adult Tobacco Survey found 21.4% of adults (199.4 million) use smokeless tobacco. Among smokeless users who saw a health care provider in the past year, only 31.7% were advised to quit, versus 48.8% of smokers. Yet half of current chewers (49.6%) were thinking of quitting and a third had tried. Chairside: every dental visit is a chance to give that advice.
cards.rib: Give every chewer clear quit advice, even when they don't ask

fig.title: Users advised to quit by a provider

cards.ev: Policy · National Oral Health Programme, DGHS MoHFW
cards.head: NOHP has funded dental units down to PHC level
cards.take: India's National Oral Health Programme, launched in 2014-15, helps states set up dental care units in district hospitals and below, with staff, chairs, autoclaves, consumables and training. DGHS reports over 9500 units supported, including more than 5000 at primary health centres. National resource centres cover potentially malignant disorders and tobacco cessation. Chairside: know your nearest government dental unit for patients who cannot pay.
cards.rib: Map the nearest government dental unit for low-income referrals

cards.head: Dental amalgam to be phased out worldwide by 2034
cards.take: At COP-6 in Geneva in November 2025, parties to the Minamata Convention on Mercury agreed that manufacture, import and export of dental amalgam will end by 2034. An exemption allows amalgam when a dentist judges it necessary for a patient. FDI and IADR stressed prevention, affordable alternatives and proper mercury waste handling. Chairside: build prevention and adhesive skills, and fit an amalgam separator.
cards.rib: Build prevention and adhesive skills, and manage amalgam waste

cards.head: Dry mouth: no spray or gel is clearly effective
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 36 trials (1597 people) tested saliva substitutes, gels, sprays, lozenges and chewing gum for dry mouth. No topical product showed strong evidence of relieving dryness; one spray beat another by about 2 points on a 10-point scale. Sugar-free gum increased saliva when some gland function remained. Chairside: review drug causes, advise sugar-free gum and water, and add fluoride.
cards.rib: Check medicines, suggest sugar-free gum and add daily fluoride

cards.head: Early Class II treatment mainly protects the incisors
cards.take: This Cochrane review of 27 trials (1251 children) found that early two-phase treatment of prominent upper incisors with a functional appliance cut incisal trauma from 30% to 19% (OR 0.56) compared with one course in adolescence. Final overjet did not differ. Functional appliances in adolescents reduced overjet by 4.6 to 5.5 mm versus no treatment. Chairside: refer early when a large overjet is trauma-prone.
cards.rib: Refer early when a large overjet puts the incisors at risk

cards.head: 38% SDF arrested half of severe early childhood caries
cards.rib: 38% SDF arrested half of severe early childhood caries
cards.take: 830 children aged 12–71 months with severe ECC; 38% silver diamine fluoride or placebo at baseline and 6 months. Lesion arrest at 3 months: 57.5% vs 18.8%. At 8 months: 50.2% vs 17.4%. Adverse events were no more common than with placebo (47.3% vs 43.3%). Bottom line: For a child who cannot sit for restorations, twice-yearly SDF is an evidence-based way to stop cavitated lesions. Warn parents about the black staining before you apply it.

cards.head: Peri-implantitis: which antibiotic adjunct works best
cards.rib: Peri-implantitis: which antibiotic adjunct works best
cards.take: Network meta-analysis of 21 clinical studies (1,718 participants). With open-flap debridement, systemic metronidazole plus amoxicillin gave the best reduction in pocket depth and marginal bone loss. Without surgery, metronidazole alone was the best adjunct for attachment level and bone loss. Local antibiotics did less than systemic ones. Bottom line: Antibiotics support decontamination; they do not replace it. Effect sizes vary, so reserve them for confirmed peri-implantitis, not mucositis.

cards.head: Calcium silicate sealer: healing keeps improving to 5 years
cards.rib: Calcium silicate sealer: healing keeps improving to 5 years
cards.take: 637 teeth with symptomatic apical periodontitis, single operator, premixed calcium silicate sealer with cold hydraulic condensation. Strict success (no symptoms, full radiographic healing) rose from 80.2% at 1 year to 87.7% at 5 years. A larger lesion at baseline (higher PAI score) was the strongest predictor of incomplete healing. Sealer extrusion did not affect outcome. Bottom line: A lesion that is smaller but not gone at one year is often still healing. Keep reviewing before you plan a retreatment or surgery.

cards.head: Root canals work as well in autoimmune disease
cards.rib: Root canals work as well in autoimmune disease
cards.take: 203 patients with autoimmune disease (317 teeth) matched with 203 controls (312 teeth), followed for about four years. Success rates did not differ between groups. The inflammatory bowel disease subgroup did worse than rheumatoid arthritis or psoriasis. Tooth type, arch and a preoperative periapical lesion predicted outcome. Autoimmune disease did not. Bottom line: An autoimmune diagnosis is not a reason to choose extraction over endodontics. Local factors decide the prognosis.

cards.ev: In vitro study · The Open Dentistry Journal 2026
cards.head: Endocrown or post and crown for a root-treated incisor
cards.rib: Endocrown or post and crown for a root-treated incisor
cards.take: 20 extracted maxillary central incisors loaded at 45° until failure. Fracture resistance did not differ significantly between the two designs. 80% of endocrown failures were repairable, compared with 60% for post-and-core. Bottom line: A lab study of 20 teeth, without thermal cycling or fatigue. The endocrown looks promising for anterior teeth, but clinical data are still needed.

cards.ev: Clinical trial · J Pharmacy & Bioallied Sciences Dec 2025
cards.head: Loupes cut root canal time and errors
cards.rib: Loupes cut root canal time and errors
cards.take: 100 patients: root canal treatment with magnifying loupes or without. Treatment time was about 25% shorter with loupes. Procedural errors were significantly fewer (P < 0.05), and patients were more satisfied. Bottom line: Loupes are an inexpensive upgrade with a measurable effect. The trial is small and its randomisation is not described, so treat the size of the effect with caution.

cards.ev: Systematic review · Clinical and Experimental Dental Research 2026
cards.head: Clear aligners are kinder to the gingiva
cards.rib: Clear aligners are kinder to the gingiva
cards.take: Systematic review of 12 studies. From one month to one year, aligner patients had less plaque, less gingival inflammation and shallower pockets. S. mutans counts were consistently lower with aligners. Bottom line: For a patient with periodontal risk, aligners make hygiene easier, mainly because they come out. Fixed-appliance patients need closer hygiene review.

cards.ev: Systematic review and meta-analysis · BMC Oral Health 2026
cards.head: LIPUS in orthodontics: not ready for routine use
cards.rib: LIPUS in orthodontics: not ready for routine use
cards.take: Meta-analysis of 11 studies of low-intensity pulsed ultrasound. Pain at 24 hours: no significant difference from controls (MD −0.76; 95% CI −2.86 to 1.33). Results on faster tooth movement ranged from substantial to negligible. Bottom line: Do not sell LIPUS to patients as faster or painless treatment yet. Standardised RCTs are needed.

cards.head: Severe periodontitis tracks with diabetic retinal change
cards.rib: Severe periodontitis tracks with diabetic retinal change
cards.take: 100 participants, from healthy controls to proliferative diabetic retinopathy, examined with OCT and OCT-angiography. Stage III–IV periodontitis was associated with thinner retinal nerve fibre layers and lower retinal vessel density. The design is cross-sectional, so it shows association, not cause. Bottom line: For a diabetic patient with advanced periodontitis, treat the gums and ask whether their yearly retinal check is up to date.

cards.ev: Lodi G et al. · Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021
cards.head: Antibiotics at extraction: what they buy, what they cost
cards.rib: Antibiotics at extraction: what they buy, what they cost
cards.take: Cochrane review, mostly third molar surgery in healthy adults. Antibiotics reduced postoperative infection by about two-thirds (NNT 19) and dry socket by about a third (NNT 46). Adverse effects were mostly brief and minor, but each prescription adds to resistance. Bottom line: Treating 19 healthy patients to prevent one infection is a poor trade for routine extractions. Reserve antibiotics for higher-risk patients and difficult surgery.

cards.head: Acute dental pain: NSAIDs first, opioids last
cards.rib: Acute dental pain: NSAIDs first, opioids last
cards.take: ADA guideline for adolescents (12 and over) and adults. NSAIDs alone, or combined with paracetamol (acetaminophen), are the first choice for pain after extraction and for toothache. Opioids are reserved for the rare case where these fail or are contraindicated. Bottom line: Ibuprofen with paracetamol relieves dental pain as well as opioid combinations, without the dependence risk.

cards.head: Toothache needs treatment, not an antibiotic
cards.rib: Toothache needs treatment, not an antibiotic
cards.take: ADA guideline for immunocompetent adults. No antibiotics for symptomatic irreversible pulpitis, or for pulp necrosis with apical periodontitis or a localised abscess. Antibiotics are for systemic involvement (fever, malaise, spreading swelling, lymphadenopathy) or when definitive treatment cannot be done. Bottom line: Pulpectomy, incision and drainage or extraction is the treatment. An antibiotic without them only delays it.

cards.head: Endocarditis prophylaxis: who still needs it
cards.rib: Endocarditis prophylaxis: who still needs it
cards.take: Only the highest-risk patients: prosthetic valves or valve repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, and cardiac transplant with valvulopathy. Only for procedures that manipulate the gingiva or periapical region, or perforate the mucosa. Amoxicillin 2 g orally, 30–60 minutes before. Clindamycin is no longer recommended. Bottom line: Rheumatic heart disease without a prosthetic valve, mitral valve prolapse or a stent does not need prophylaxis under this guidance. When unsure, ask the cardiologist.

cards.ev: Sanz M et al. · J Clin Periodontol 2020
cards.head: The EFP four-step treatment of periodontitis
cards.rib: The EFP four-step treatment of periodontitis
cards.take: Step 1: oral hygiene instruction, risk factor control (stop smoking, control diabetes) and supragingival cleaning. Step 2: subgingival instrumentation. Systemic antibiotics are not routine; consider them only in specific young patients with severe disease. Step 3: re-evaluate, then treat residual pockets (4 mm or deeper with bleeding, or 6 mm or deeper). Step 4: supportive care every 3–12 months. Bottom line: The re-evaluation visit is what most practices skip. Book it before the patient leaves after step 2.

cards.head: Edentulous mandible: two implants make the denture
cards.rib: Edentulous mandible: two implants make the denture
cards.take: The McGill consensus statement made the two-implant overdenture the minimum standard of care for the edentulous mandible. It gives better retention, chewing and satisfaction than a conventional complete denture. Two implants cost far less than a fixed full-arch prosthesis. Bottom line: Offer it to every patient struggling with a lower denture. It is often the most cost-effective implant treatment in the practice.

cards.ev: Ruggiero SL et al. · J Oral Maxillofac Surg 2022
cards.head: Extraction in a patient on bisphosphonates
cards.rib: Extraction in a patient on bisphosphonates
cards.take: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ) is far less common at osteoporosis doses than at the doses used for cancer. Before starting cancer-dose antiresorptives, complete dental treatment and let extraction sites heal. Evidence for stopping the drug before extraction (a 'drug holiday') remains limited. Talk to the prescribing physician. Bottom line: Do not refuse a needed extraction to an osteoporosis patient. Extract atraumatically, close primarily where possible, and review healing.

cards.head: National Dental Commission replaces the DCI
cards.rib: National Dental Commission replaces the DCI
cards.take: The National Dental Commission Act, 2023 was notified in March 2026. Dental graduates will have to pass the National Exit Test (NExT) to practise. It is to be introduced within three years. State dental council heads will now be appointed by state governments, and the Commission can regulate fees for half the seats in private colleges. Bottom line: Registered practitioners keep their registration. Watch for the NExT schedule if you teach or employ new graduates.
